title: I used AI to help build a jetpack llama game where going faster makes destroying shit easier. Here's what I learned.
author: SpookJr88
selftext:
I've been building a deliberately ridiculous arcade game called **Flying Llama Drama**.

The loop is simple: go fast, smash stuff, build combos, and keep accelerating until everything gets increasingly stupid.

**GO FAST. BREAK STUFF. DON'T HIT THE BUS.**

AI has been part of the development workflow rather than something running inside the game. I've used AI assistants for coding, debugging, troubleshooting, iteration, and parts of the promotional workflow. I still make the gameplay and product decisions, test the actual builds, reject plenty of bad ideas, and decide what ultimately ships.

One thing that's surprised me is how much the bottleneck changes. AI can help me implement and iterate much faster, but it doesn't magically answer **“is this actually fun?”** That still comes down to playing it, watching what works, changing mechanics, and getting feedback from actual people.

This is the first gameplay trailer, and I'm still working toward release.

For other people building games with AI: **where have you found AI genuinely speeds up development, and where does human judgment/testing still become the bottleneck?**

Also, if you watch the gameplay, I'd love to know whether the core idea reads immediately or whether I'm too close to it now.

comments.author: hushzephyr
comments.body: Simple mechanics, but it still feels satisfying enough. This direction should be solid.
